response.question: My neighbour filed a police complaint accusing me of stealing his expensive laptop. I have CCTV footage proving that I was not even present at his house that day. What can I do against a false criminal complaint? Can I take legal action against him?
response.answer:
Yes, legal action may be possible, but it depends on the facts. Your CCTV footage may help you respond to the accusation. It does not, by itself, establish that your neighbour knew the complaint was false.

Under BNS section 217, giving a public servant information that the person knows or believes is false can be an offence if the required intention or knowledge about the public servant’s action is present. This includes intending or knowing it is likely that the public servant will use their lawful power to injure or annoy someone. The available source does not explain how to start a prosecution under this section.

Compensation may also be possible in certain circumstances. If you are accused before a Magistrate in a case the Magistrate can try, and are later discharged or acquitted, the Magistrate may consider compensation if they find there was no reasonable ground for the accusation. The complainant must have an opportunity to explain, and compensation is not automatic.

response.question: Police officers came to my house and arrested my brother without explaining the reason. They have not allowed us to contact a lawyer or informed us about where he is being taken. What are his legal rights after arrest, and what can our family do?
response.answer:
I’m sorry your family is facing this. The information available does not establish whether the police explained the arrest to your brother or whether they had a warrant. His rights include:

• If he was arrested without a warrant, the officer must promptly tell him the full details of the alleged offence or other grounds for arrest.
• If police interrogate him, he can meet a lawyer of his choice during questioning, though the lawyer need not be present throughout.
• The person making the arrest must promptly inform a relative, friend or other person your brother identifies or nominates about the arrest and where he is being held. At the police station, he must be told of this right.
• The arresting officer must prepare an arrest memorandum—a record of the arrest—witnessed as specified in the law and countersigned by your brother.
• If he was arrested without a warrant, police must take or send him without unnecessary delay before the appropriate Magistrate or the officer in charge of a police station. A Magistrate is a judicial officer.
• If he was arrested under a warrant, he must be brought before the required court without unnecessary delay. The delay cannot exceed 24 hours, excluding necessary travel time to the Magistrate’s court.
• If he was arrested without a warrant and is not accused of a non-bailable offence, police must tell him that he can be released on bail and arrange sureties—people who provide assurance for his release.

These sources do not set out a general 24-hour deadline for every arrest without a warrant. A lawyer can help check the circumstances urgently.

response.question: Three people attacked me while I was walking home at night. I hit one of them with a nearby object to escape, and he suffered serious injuries. Can I claim the right of private defence under Indian criminal law? Could I still be arrested?
response.answer:
I’m sorry this happened to you. You may be able to claim private defence: the law recognises a right to defend your body against an attack. Whether it applies depends on the circumstances, including what danger you reasonably feared and what you did to escape.

You must not cause more harm than necessary for defence. The right lasts while a reasonable fear of danger to your body continues. It does not apply where there is time to seek protection from public authorities. If an assault reasonably makes you fear death or serious injury, the right can extend to causing serious harm to the attacker, subject to those restrictions. An act done within the right of private defence is not an offence.

I cannot say from the available sources whether you could be arrested: they do not provide the rules on arrest. The fact that three people attacked you does not, by itself, settle whether your response was within the right of private defence.

response.question: Someone posted false allegations about me on Instagram, claiming that I committed fraud. The post has damaged my reputation and affected my professional opportunities. Can I file a criminal defamation case in India? What remedies are available?
response.answer:
Yes. You may make a criminal defamation complaint about the Instagram post. An allegation can amount to defamation if it was published with intent to harm your reputation, or with knowledge or reason to believe it would do so. The court would consider the evidence and any applicable exceptions. [bns_2023:356]

For example, the law makes an exception for a true allegation published for the public good. Other exceptions may also apply. [bns_2023:356]

As the person affected, you may complain to a Magistrate with jurisdiction. A Magistrate is a judicial officer who hears certain criminal cases. [bnss_2023:222]

If defamation is established, the possible punishment is simple imprisonment for up to two years, a fine, both, or community service. A fine is not necessarily compensation paid to you. [bns_2023:356]

The sources provided do not explain whether you can obtain compensation or a court order to remove the post. A lawyer can help you explore those questions.

response.question: My former friend is threatening to leak my private photographs unless I pay him ₹50,000. He has sent these threats over WhatsApp. What criminal provisions protect me, and what should I do immediately?
response.answer:
I’m sorry this is happening to you. You can seek help now; you do not need to wait for the photographs to be shared.

• The threat to obtain money may fall under BNS section 308(3), which covers putting or attempting to put someone in fear of injury in order to commit extortion [bns_2023:308].
• BNS section 308(1) defines extortion as using fear to dishonestly induce someone to hand over property, including money. Whether you have paid is relevant to this distinction [bns_2023:308].
• If the images show a private area and were captured, published or electronically sent without consent in circumstances violating privacy, IT Act section 66E may also apply. A threat to share alone does not establish that this provision applies [it_act_2000:66E].

These are possible provisions, not a prediction of the outcome. This is legal information, not legal advice.

response.question: My manager keeps making sexual comments and hinted that my promotion depends on 'being friendly' with him. Our company has about 30 employees. Where and how do I complain, and is there a time limit?
response.answer:
I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. If the sexual comments were unwelcome, they may amount to sexual harassment. A hint that promotion depends on such conduct may also be relevant [posh_act_2013:2; posh_act_2013:3].

The workplace complaint route below applies if you are a woman [posh_act_2013:2; posh_act_2013:9]:

• Your employer must set up an Internal Committee to handle workplace sexual harassment complaints [posh_act_2013:4]. You can submit a written complaint to it. If no Internal Committee has been set up, you can complain to the Local Committee [posh_act_2013:9].
• If you cannot write the complaint yourself, a committee officer or member must give you reasonable help to put it in writing [posh_act_2013:9].
• The usual time limit is three months from the incident, or three months from the last incident in a series. The committee may allow up to three more months if circumstances prevented you from filing on time; it must record its reasons in writing [posh_act_2013:9].

The sources provided do not explain this workplace complaint route for someone who is not a woman. A qualified lawyer can help you explore your options.

response.question: My friend was sexually assaulted by someone she knows. She is scared of going to the police station. Can she report it without going there, and will her name be published?
response.answer:
I’m sorry this happened to your friend. It is understandable that she is scared.

**Reporting without visiting a police station:** Information about a cognizable offence—an offence for which police may arrest without a warrant—can be sent electronically to the officer in charge of a police station. The person giving it must sign it within three days for it to be taken on record. The available sources do not say that the entire reporting process can always be completed without a station visit. [bnss_2023:173, bnss_2023:2]

If the offence is rape, her statement is to be recorded at her home or another place she chooses. As far as practicable, a woman police officer should record it, in the presence of a parent, guardian, near relative or local social worker. [bnss_2023:176]

**Her name:** The available sources do not answer whether her name can be published in this situation. I cannot promise that it will or will not be published. A qualified lawyer can explain the privacy protections that apply to her circumstances.

response.question: I am a school teacher. A 12-year-old student told me that a relative touches her inappropriately. Do I have to report this to the police? What happens if I don't?
response.answer:
I’m sorry your student has shared this. She is a child, and her safety matters.

Yes. If you understand from what she told you that a sexual offence has happened or is likely to happen, you must report the information to the local police or the Special Juvenile Police Unit, a police unit for children. You do not need to decide yourself whether the relative is guilty. The law protects a person from civil or criminal liability for giving the information in good faith.

The sources available to me do not say what penalty, if any, applies if you do not report. I cannot answer that part from the laws available.

response.question: I belong to a Scheduled Caste. Some people in my village insulted me using my caste name in front of everyone and are stopping my family from using the village water source. Which law protects me?
response.answer:
I’m sorry this happened to you. The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 may protect you.

Under this Act, abusing a Scheduled Caste person by caste name in a place within public view can be an offence. Preventing a Scheduled Caste person from using a common water source can also be an offence. These provisions apply when the person responsible is not a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe. Whether they apply in your case depends on the facts.

The Act also says the State must make arrangements to protect victims, their dependents and witnesses against threats or violence.

response.question: The police station near my house refused to register my FIR, saying the incident happened in another area's jurisdiction. Are they allowed to do that?
response.answer:
No—not just because the incident happened in another area, if the information concerns a cognizable offence. A cognizable offence is one for which police may arrest without a warrant. You can give this information to the officer in charge of a police station, regardless of where the offence happened. The recorded information must be given to you or the victim free of cost.

If the officer in charge refuses to record it, you can send the information in writing and by post to the Superintendent of Police concerned. If that does not resolve the matter, you may apply to a Magistrate. The sources do not establish whether your particular incident is a cognizable offence.
